items.title: From Rochester to Atlanta to Wilkes-Barre to Mohegan Sun: The Vacation That Forgot Where It Was Going
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are plenty of things that can go wrong when traveling. Flights get delayed, luggage gets lost, hotels turn out to be considerably less impressive than their photographs, and occasionally you end up spending $20 on a restaurant meal that tastes like something you could have purchased in the frozen-food section of a grocery store. Those things happen. They’re part of traveling.

But there are certain travel experiences that are so ridiculous that they deserve to be remembered for years. Being forced to land in a city you never intended to visit, having no convenient way to get out, struggling to find food, discovering that there is practically nothing to do on a Saturday night, and eventually considering just about any transportation option that might get you somewhere else certainly qualifies.

Our original plan was simple: travel from Rochester, New York, to Atlanta, Georgia. That was the destination. Atlanta was where we were supposed to be going, and Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, wasn’t even remotely part of the itinerary. We weren’t looking for a Pennsylvania vacation, weren’t researching hotels in northeastern Pennsylvania, and certainly weren’t trying to find the best Italian restaurant in Wilkes-Barre.

We had no reason to be there.

Then the FAA entered the picture.

For reasons that resulted in us having to land, the aircraft was grounded in Wilkes-Barre. Just like that, our trip took an entirely different direction. We went from traveling toward Atlanta to being stuck in a Pennsylvania city that we had never intended to visit in the first place.

There is something particularly frustrating about being stranded somewhere you didn’t choose. If you book a vacation and decide to visit a particular city, you generally have some idea of what you’re getting into. You research hotels, look at restaurants, find attractions, and make plans. Even if the destination isn’t everything you hoped it would be, at least you chose to go there.

We didn’t choose Wilkes-Barre.

The FAA essentially made that decision for us.

And while the original circumstances of the grounding were beyond our control, everything that followed seemed to involve another unnecessary complication. Transportation became a problem. We had to share a car with a completely random dude just to get to the Holiday Inn. Once there, we discovered that finding food wasn’t particularly convenient. There was practically nothing nearby, DoorDash wasn’t much help, and eventually we had to walk approximately a mile to find an Italian restaurant.

That restaurant turned out to be a disappointment of almost historic proportions. For approximately $20, we received something that was essentially a Lean Cuisine dinner. After walking a mile to get there, we might as well have gone to a grocery store, purchased a frozen meal, and heated it up in the hotel room.

Saturday night wasn’t any better. We desperately tried to find something to do, but there was absolutely nothing that appealed to us. We searched for entertainment, considered possibilities, and eventually surrendered to watching the Sharter Show because apparently that was the best Wilkes-Barre had to offer.

We even explored just about every possible way of getting out of town, including the possibility of taking a bus with a bunch of older passengers. When you’re considering transportation options you might never have entertained under normal circumstances simply because you want to escape your current location, you know the situation has become ridiculous.

Somehow, though, there were a few unexpected bright spots. We managed to catch Arrested Development, which was a pretty good surprise considering the circumstances. And while Wilkes-Barre was doing its best to make us regret ever having heard of the place, we eventually managed to turn the situation into a collection of stories that would be considerably funnier in retrospect than they were while we were living through them.

This wasn’t a planned vacation. It wasn’t a sightseeing adventure. It wasn’t some elaborate trip through Pennsylvania.

It was a trip from Rochester to Atlanta that got hijacked by circumstances beyond our control.

And Wilkes-Barre was where the adventure went off the rails.

The Original Plan: Getting from Rochester to Atlanta

The journey began with a destination in mind and absolutely no expectation that Wilkes-Barre would become part of the story.

Rochester to Atlanta. That was the plan.

There was no reason to think we would end up spending an extended amount of time in northeastern Pennsylvania. We weren’t looking for somewhere to spend a weekend, and we certainly weren’t searching for recommendations about where to eat in Wilkes-Barre.

Atlanta was the destination. Everything else was supposed to be part of getting there.

That’s generally how traveling works. You make arrangements, figure out how you’re getting where you need to go, and expect that the transportation system will get you reasonably close to the intended destination. There might be a delay or an inconvenience, but you don’t generally expect to be deposited in an entirely different city and then have to figure out what happens next.

Unfortunately, that is exactly what happened.

The FAA forced the aircraft to land in Wilkes-Barre, and suddenly our original itinerary was meaningless.

There is a difference between choosing to make an unexpected stop and having one imposed on you. If you’re driving and see an interesting town, you can decide to pull over, explore, get something to eat, and continue when you’re ready. That’s part of the fun of traveling.

Being forced to land somewhere is a completely different experience.

You aren’t stopping because you discovered a wonderful attraction. You aren’t stopping because somebody recommended an amazing restaurant. You aren’t stopping because you decided that the town looked interesting.

You’re stopping because you have to.

And when you find yourself in a city you never intended to visit, the first question is generally not, “What exciting attractions are available?”

It’s, “How do we get out of here?”

That became the central theme of the entire experience.

We had gone from having a straightforward destination to having no particularly clear idea what the next steps would be. We needed somewhere to stay, transportation to that location, food, and eventually some way to continue moving toward where we originally intended to go.

None of those things sounded especially complicated individually.

Together, however, they would become an unexpectedly entertaining collection of travel disasters.

There are plenty of reasons people end up making unexpected stops while traveling, but getting grounded by the FAA is certainly not something you put on your vacation checklist.

You can prepare for a lot of things. You can bring extra clothes, make sure your phone is charged, keep some money available, and research alternate transportation. But you don’t necessarily expect that a trip from Rochester to Atlanta will suddenly involve an unplanned landing in Wilkes-Barre.

The problem with an unexpected landing is that it doesn’t automatically solve anything beyond getting you on the ground.

You still have to figure out where you’re going to stay, how you’re going to get there, what you’re going to eat, and how you’re going to continue your journey.

And if you’re somewhere you never intended to visit, you may not know anything about the surrounding area.

That’s where we found ourselves.

We hadn’t researched Wilkes-Barre because there was no reason to research Wilkes-Barre. We hadn’t selected a hotel based on its proximity to restaurants or entertainment. We didn’t have a list of attractions to visit or a collection of transportation options ready to go.

We were suddenly dealing with a destination that hadn’t existed in our plans a few hours earlier.

The whole situation was a reminder that travel doesn’t always care what you’ve arranged. You can have a destination, a schedule, and a perfectly reasonable expectation of how the day is supposed to unfold, and then something outside your control changes everything.

The FAA had made its decision, and we had to deal with the consequences.

The immediate problem was getting situated.

We needed a hotel, and we needed transportation to get there.

That brings us to one of the more unusual parts of the entire experience.

Sharing a Car with a Completely Random Dude

Getting to the Holiday Inn wasn’t exactly a straightforward operation.

We somehow ended up sharing a car with a completely random dude.

That’s right. After being unexpectedly grounded in a city we never planned to visit, one of the next adventures involved climbing into a vehicle with somebody we didn’t know just to get to the hotel.

It wasn’t exactly the glamorous beginning to a Pennsylvania vacation that nobody had requested.

Most people imagine arriving somewhere, collecting their luggage, getting into a waiting vehicle, and heading to their hotel. Everything is reasonably organized, and you can concentrate on getting settled.

Our experience was a little different.

We were trying to sort out transportation in an unfamiliar place, and the solution involved sharing a ride with a stranger.

There is something inherently funny about how quickly your expectations change when travel doesn’t go according to plan.

Under normal circumstances, you might have a list of requirements for transportation. You want something convenient, comfortable, and reasonably direct. You might compare different options or choose the easiest arrangement.

When you’ve just been forced to land somewhere you never intended to visit, the priorities become considerably simpler.

Does it get us to the hotel?

We weren’t trying to arrange a luxury transportation experience. We just needed to get where we were going.

So we shared the car with the random dude and made our way to the Holiday Inn.

At least that part worked.

We had transportation, we arrived at the hotel, and we could finally concentrate on figuring out the next part of the adventure.

Unfortunately, the hotel location was about to introduce us to another problem.

The Holiday Inn: Welcome to Nowhere

There are hotels that are conveniently located near everything you might need, and then there are hotels where you quickly discover that the surrounding area offers very little in the way of convenient options.

The Holiday Inn in Wilkes-Barre was not exactly giving us the impression that we had arrived in the center of a thriving entertainment district.

We weren’t expecting the hotel to be surrounded by luxury restaurants and expensive shopping. We just wanted somewhere reasonably convenient to get food and perhaps find something to do.

That seemed like a fairly modest expectation.

But once we were settled, the immediate problem became apparent.

There wasn’t much nearby.

This is one of those things that can make a tremendous difference when you’re traveling. If you have a car, you can generally get around the problem. A restaurant might be several miles away, but that’s not necessarily an issue if you can simply drive there.

When you don’t have that convenience, location becomes extremely important.

A restaurant that is five miles away might as well be on another continent if you don’t have a convenient way to reach it.

And that’s essentially how the situation started to feel.

We were at the Holiday Inn, but being at the hotel didn’t mean we had easy access to anything else.

Finding food was going to require some planning.

Finding entertainment would require even more.

And getting out of town was becoming a separate transportation challenge.

It wasn’t exactly the relaxing experience you imagine when you think about a hotel stay.

We hadn’t chosen this location because we wanted to explore Wilkes-Barre. We hadn’t spent weeks researching the surrounding neighborhood. We were there because the FAA had forced an unexpected change in our plans, and we needed somewhere to stay.

The hotel was a temporary solution to a problem we hadn’t anticipated.

Unfortunately, temporary solutions have a way of becoming considerably less appealing when you discover that everything you need is somewhere else.

The Great DoorDash Disappointment

Normally, when you’re staying at a hotel and don’t feel like going anywhere, food delivery is a pretty good option.

You open an app, look through the available restaurants, find something that sounds decent, place an order, and wait for dinner to arrive.

It’s one of the conveniences that makes traveling easier.

You don’t need a car. You don’t need to navigate an unfamiliar area. You don’t have to figure out where restaurants are located or how far away they might be.

Unfortunately, DoorDash wasn’t going to provide the easy solution we were hoping for.

The nearby options weren’t particularly useful, and the entire process became another reminder that we weren’t staying somewhere especially convenient.

We weren’t looking for anything complicated. We didn’t need some exclusive dining experience or a restaurant with a celebrity chef.

A pizza would have been fine. A decent sandwich would have been fine. Something delivered to the hotel without requiring an elaborate transportation arrangement would have been even better.

But apparently, even that was going to be difficult.

The delivery situation wasn’t helping, and the nearby restaurant situation wasn’t much better.

Eventually, we had to accept that if we wanted dinner, we were going to have to go out and find it ourselves.

A Mile for Dinner: The Wilkes-Barre Walking Tour Nobody Requested

There are plenty of reasons to take a walk when you’re traveling.

You might be exploring a new city, enjoying the scenery, checking out interesting neighborhoods, or simply getting some exercise.

Walking a mile because there is nowhere convenient to get dinner is a different experience.

That’s what we ended up doing.

Approximately one mile just to find something to eat.

It sounds almost ridiculous when you think about it. We were staying at a hotel, and rather than having a selection of restaurants nearby, we had to make a fairly substantial walk to locate somewhere to eat.

Nobody was asking for a five-star dining experience. We weren’t trying to discover some hidden culinary destination. We just wanted a meal.

The problem was that the immediate area wasn’t giving us many options.

And eventually found an Italian restaurant.

At that point, we were hoping that the effort would be worthwhile. After everything that had happened, a decent dinner would have been a welcome improvement.

We had already been forced to land in an unexpected city, dealt with transportation problems, shared a car with a random stranger, and discovered that our hotel wasn’t particularly convenient for finding food.

Surely dinner could go right.

Surely we could have one ordinary, enjoyable experience.

Wilkes-Barre had one more surprise waiting.

The Italian Restaurant: Twenty Dollars for Something from the Frozen Food Section

The Italian restaurant deserves its own section because the meal was almost too ridiculous to forget.

After walking approximately a mile, we finally arrived at a place that looked like it might provide a reasonable dinner.

Italian food is generally a pretty dependable choice. You can find good Italian restaurants in almost any city, and even a relatively simple restaurant can serve a satisfying meal.

Pasta, sauce, perhaps some chicken, and a little bread.

It isn’t exactly rocket science.

We weren’t expecting an elaborate dining experience. We just wanted something that tasted like it had been prepared in an actual restaurant.

Instead, we ended up with what was essentially a Lean Cuisine for $20.

Those little frozen meals you find in the grocery store. The ones you purchase when you’re too tired to cook, take home, put in the microwave, and eat while wondering why you didn’t just order a pizza.

That was essentially the experience.

Except this version required walking a mile, sitting in a restaurant, and paying approximately $20.

There is something particularly insulting about spending restaurant money on food that looks like it should come with instructions telling you to remove the plastic film before microwaving.

You almost have to admire the accomplishment.

We had gone through all the trouble of finding the place, getting there, sitting down, ordering, and waiting for dinner.

And after all that, we were left with something that probably would have been just as satisfying if we’d purchased it at Walmart.

At least we could have eaten it in the hotel room without making the one-mile journey.

The entire experience became another example of how nothing about the Wilkes-Barre portion of the trip seemed to be working in our favor.

The transportation was inconvenient.

The hotel location wasn’t particularly useful.

DoorDash wasn’t solving the problem.

And when we finally found a restaurant, the meal wasn’t worth the effort.

At this point, Wilkes-Barre was building a pretty impressive record.

We had arrived there against our wishes, and the town seemed to be doing everything possible to make sure we didn’t develop any affection for it.

The food certainly wasn’t helping.

And then Saturday night arrived.

Saturday Night: We Just Wanted Something to Do

There is something particularly disappointing about spending a Saturday night somewhere and discovering that you have absolutely no interest in any of the available entertainment options.

When you’re traveling, Saturday night is usually an opportunity to get out and enjoy yourself.

You might find a bar, catch some live music, visit a restaurant, or simply walk around and see what’s happening.

It doesn’t have to be complicated.

Sometimes the best part of traveling is discovering something you weren’t expecting.

A great little restaurant, a local music venue, an interesting neighborhood, or a bar where you end up spending several hours having a good time.

We were hoping for something along those lines.

Instead, we were in Wilkes-Barre.

And we were desperate to find something to do.

Not looking for one or two possibilities.

We genuinely wanted to get out of the hotel and do something entertaining.

After everything else that had happened, we were ready for a little normality.

A decent bar would have been fine.

Live music would have been great.

A restaurant with some atmosphere would have worked.

Even a place to grab a drink and sit around for a while would have been an improvement.

But we searched and searched, and there was absolutely nothing that seemed worth the effort.

You know how sometimes you search for things to do in a city and find dozens of possibilities?

You start narrowing them down.

Maybe this place looks interesting. Maybe that bar has live music. Maybe there’s an event happening downtown.

We weren’t having that experience.

We were struggling to find even one thing that made us want to leave the hotel.

And the more we looked, the more absurd the situation became.

We had been forced to land in a city we never intended to visit.

And now we couldn’t even find anything entertaining to do.

At some point, you stop wondering what you’re missing and start accepting that the options simply aren’t appealing.

Wilkes-Barre was not exactly making a strong case for itself as a weekend destination.

The Sharter Show: Our Saturday Night Entertainment

We had searched for something to do, considered the possibilities, and reached the conclusion that there was absolutely nothing worth going out for.

And that’s how we ended up watching the Sharter Show.

After everything involved in getting to Wilkes-Barre, our Saturday-night entertainment consisted of watching television in the hotel room.

It’s difficult to imagine a more appropriate ending to the day.

We hadn’t chosen to stay in because we were exhausted from an exciting day of sightseeing. We weren’t relaxing after visiting a collection of interesting attractions.

We were simply out of options.

There was nothing we wanted to go see, nowhere we particularly wanted to visit, and no compelling reason to leave the hotel.

So we watched the Sharter Show.

If somebody had told us at the beginning of the trip that this would be how we spent Saturday night, it probably would have sounded like a joke.

We were supposed to be traveling from Rochester to Atlanta.

Instead, we were grounded in Wilkes-Barre, walking a mile for dinner, paying $20 for a frozen-food-quality Italian meal, and watching the Sharter Show because the town had apparently run out of entertainment.

It’s the kind of thing you can’t really plan.

And it’s also the kind of thing that makes a trip memorable.

The funny part is that we weren’t even particularly difficult to entertain. We weren’t demanding a major concert or a professional sporting event.

We just wanted something to do.

Instead, Saturday night ended up being a hotel-room television experience.

At least we had something to laugh about.

Operation: Get Us Out of Wilkes-Barre

By this point, the biggest priority was finding a way to leave.

We had never intended to be there, and the longer the situation continued, the more we wanted to move on.

The original journey was Rochester to Atlanta. That was where we were supposed to be going.

Wilkes-Barre was an interruption, not a destination.

And it was becoming an interruption that was difficult to get past.

The transportation situation made everything more complicated.

We didn’t have a convenient car sitting outside the hotel. We couldn’t simply get in and drive to another city. We didn’t have an easy train option that would solve the problem, and flying wasn’t going to provide a practical answer to every short-distance transportation question.

We were left looking at whatever options were available.

And when you’re stuck somewhere you don’t want to be, you become considerably less particular about how you leave.

Normally, you might compare transportation options based on comfort, schedule, convenience, and cost.

At this point, the criteria were much simpler.

Does it get us out of Wilkes-Barre?

The idea of taking a bus became part of the discussion.

And not necessarily some luxurious bus experience with comfortable seats and a relaxing journey.

We were even considering a bus with a bunch of older passengers.

At that point, who cared?

If it got us somewhere else, it was worth considering.

There is a certain desperation involved in reaching the point where you’re willing to accept almost any reasonable transportation arrangement simply because you want to leave.

We weren’t looking for a sightseeing tour.

We weren’t trying to experience the local transportation system for fun.

We were looking for an escape route.

The Bus with the Older Passengers

The bus idea deserves a mention because it illustrates just how far the transportation situation had drifted from the original plan.

Think about the journey we had started with.

Somewhere along the way, the FAA forced us to land in Wilkes-Barre, and now we were considering a bus with a group of older passengers as a possible way to get moving again.

It’s not exactly the kind of transportation planning you see in travel brochures.

Nobody starts a trip thinking, “I really hope I get to spend part of this adventure figuring out whether I can get on a bus with a bunch of older people.”

But that’s what happens when the usual transportation options aren’t available.

You start looking at alternatives.

And then you start looking at alternatives to the alternatives.

Eventually, almost anything that gets you out of the situation becomes interesting.

The whole thing was particularly frustrating because none of this was part of our original plan.

We hadn’t chosen to spend time in Wilkes-Barre. We hadn’t booked the Holiday Inn because we wanted to explore the surrounding area. We hadn’t researched restaurants or entertainment.

We were simply trying to continue a journey that had been interrupted.

And every time we thought we had found a way forward, another transportation question seemed to appear.

It was becoming less about enjoying the trip and more about managing the logistics.

Still, there was one unexpected bright spot in the middle of all this.

A Surprise Worth Leaving the Hotel For: Arrested Development

Somehow, we managed to catch Arrested Development.

And unlike the Italian restaurant, this was a discovery that actually turned out to be worthwhile.

The group became one of the most distinctive names in hip-hop during the early 1990s, arriving at a time when the genre was expanding in several different directions.

Their debut album, 3 Years, 5 Months and 2 Days in the Life Of…, introduced a sound that was considerably different from much of the hardcore rap and gangsta rap that dominated the conversation during that period.

Led by Speech, Arrested Development combined hip-hop with elements of funk, soul, gospel, and socially conscious songwriting.

Songs like “Tennessee,” “People Everyday,” and “Mr. Wendal” helped establish the group as a major name in alternative hip-hop.

The group was particularly interesting because it didn’t follow the same formula as many of its contemporaries. Their music had a different perspective, a different sound, and a different approach to the subject matter.

They were part of a movement that demonstrated just how broad hip-hop could be.

Their success was significant, and their debut album received widespread recognition. The group eventually became one of the defining acts of the alternative hip-hop movement.

Catching them during this unexpected journey was a nice surprise.

It wasn’t something we had planned around the trip. We hadn’t set out to see Arrested Development. We were simply making the most of whatever opportunities came along.

And after the transportation headaches, disappointing food, and Saturday-night entertainment disaster, a live music opportunity was certainly welcome.

It was also a reminder that unexpected detours aren’t always bad.

Sometimes you end up discovering something worthwhile in the middle of an otherwise ridiculous experience.

Arrested Development gave us one of those moments.

And it was considerably better than watching the Sharter Show.

Hip-Hop Was an Unexpected Highlight

There is something particularly enjoyable about seeing a band or artist you weren’t necessarily expecting to see.

When you plan a concert trip around a particular performer, you know what you’re getting into. You research the setlists, look at the venue, and anticipate the songs you hope to hear.

When a concert happens unexpectedly, the experience can be different.

You might not know exactly what the performance will be like. You might not have been following the artist particularly closely. You simply recognize an opportunity and decide to take advantage of it.

That was the appeal of catching Arrested Development.

Their music occupies an interesting place in hip-hop history.

The early 1990s were an important period for the genre. Rap was becoming increasingly mainstream, but there was also a tremendous amount of experimentation happening outside the biggest commercial acts.

Some groups focused on harder-edged street narratives. Others explored jazz, funk, soul, political commentary, or more personal songwriting.

Arrested Development stood out because of its combination of musical influences and positive, socially conscious perspective.

“Tennessee” remains one of the group’s most recognizable recordings. “People Everyday” demonstrated its ability to take an existing musical idea and transform it into something distinctly its own. “Mr. Wendal” offered a different perspective on homelessness and social inequality.

These weren’t simply songs designed to fit into a particular commercial trend.

They helped establish an identity.

And seeing a group with that kind of history was a nice addition to a trip that had already taken several unexpected turns.

It was one of those moments where you could stop thinking about the transportation problems for a while and simply enjoy the music.

That was something we could certainly use.

The Strange Economics of Being Stuck Somewhere

One thing you quickly discover when travel plans go wrong is that even ordinary activities become more expensive and inconvenient.

When you’re in a familiar city, you know where things are. You might have friends nearby, transportation options you understand, and a general idea of where to go for food.

When you’re unexpectedly stranded somewhere, you lose much of that familiarity.

You don’t necessarily know which restaurants are good, which neighborhoods are convenient, or how to get around.

You start making decisions based on limited information.

And sometimes those decisions turn out to be terrible.

The Italian restaurant was a perfect example.

We needed food, the options were limited, and we eventually walked a mile to find something that sounded reasonably appealing.

And then we realized that the entire experience had been a waste of time compared with what we could have done if we had been somewhere with better options.

The $20 Lean Cuisine became a symbol of the entire Wilkes-Barre experience.

It wasn’t just about the food.

It was about the effort required to find it, the lack of alternatives, and the disappointment of finally getting somewhere only to discover that it wasn’t worth the trouble.

The same thing happened with entertainment.

We wanted to go out Saturday night, but the options weren’t appealing.

We spent time searching, trying to find something, and eventually gave up.

When you’re traveling, time is valuable. You don’t want to spend an entire evening researching activities that you probably won’t enjoy.

You want to be out experiencing something.

Unfortunately, that wasn’t how the Wilkes-Barre portion of the trip unfolded.

A City We Never Intended to Visit

The biggest irony is that Wilkes-Barre never had to impress us.

We hadn’t chosen it as a destination.

We weren’t expecting to spend a vacation there.

We didn’t have a bucket list of attractions to visit.

We were simply there because the FAA forced the aircraft to land.

That distinction is important.

This wasn’t a situation where we researched the city, decided it looked interesting, and then became disappointed when it didn’t meet our expectations.

We never wanted to be there in the first place.

And after spending time trying to navigate the transportation situation, find food, and locate entertainment, we weren’t developing any new appreciation for the place.

If anything, we were becoming increasingly motivated to leave.

The town had managed to turn a straightforward journey into an unexpected collection of logistical problems.

And while there may be plenty of people who enjoy living in Wilkes-Barre, our particular experience wasn’t giving us many reasons to become enthusiastic visitors.

The transportation problems were frustrating.

The hotel location was inconvenient.

The food was disappointing.

Saturday-night entertainment was practically nonexistent from our perspective.

And the only reason we were there was because the FAA had made the landing necessary.

It was an unwanted stop that became a much bigger part of the journey than anybody could have anticipated.

Looking Back at the Whole Experience

When you look back at a trip like this, it’s interesting how the memories become organized.

You might initially remember the inconvenience, the frustration, and the amount of time spent trying to figure out what to do next.

But eventually, those experiences become stories.

The random guy who shared the car ride.

The Holiday Inn with practically nothing nearby.

The mile-long walk for dinner.

The Italian restaurant that served a $20 Lean Cuisine.

The Saturday night when we couldn’t find anything to do.

The idea of taking a bus with a bunch of older passengers just to get out of town.

And then the unexpected opportunity to catch Arrested Development.

It’s a pretty unusual collection of memories.

None of them was part of the original plan, but all of them became part of the trip.

And perhaps that’s what makes the story so memorable.

We didn’t set out to create an elaborate travel adventure. We were simply trying to get from Rochester to Atlanta.

Wilkes-Barre became an unexpected stop, and everything that followed was an exercise in improvisation.

Final Thoughts: The FAA Owed Us a Better Destination

Travel is supposed to be about getting somewhere, discovering new places, and enjoying experiences along the way.

Sometimes it works out perfectly.

And sometimes the FAA forces you to land in Wilkes-Barre, and suddenly the entire trip becomes an exercise in figuring out how to survive the unexpected detour.

We started out in Rochester with Atlanta as the destination.

Instead, we found ourselves in a city we never planned to visit, sharing a car with a random stranger, staying at a Holiday Inn with very little nearby, and trying to find basic conveniences that should have been considerably easier to locate.

We walked a mile for dinner and received a $20 meal that resembled a Lean Cuisine.

We couldn’t find a decent DoorDash solution.

Saturday night offered so little entertainment that we eventually watched the Sharter Show.

We desperately looked for ways to get out of town, even considering a bus with a bunch of older passengers.

And somehow, through all of this, we managed to catch Arrested Development.

There were certainly worse ways to spend an unexpected detour, but there were also considerably better ones.

The best part is that we never intended any of it to happen.

We weren’t planning a Pennsylvania vacation. We weren’t looking for an opportunity to explore Wilkes-Barre. We weren’t trying to discover its restaurants or nightlife.

We were trying to get to Atlanta.

Instead, the FAA made Wilkes-Barre part of our story, and the town did not exactly make a convincing argument for extending the visit.

If nothing else, we learned a few things.

First, always appreciate having transportation available. You never know when you’ll find yourself somewhere you didn’t intend to visit and suddenly have to investigate every possible way of getting out.

Second, research the hotel location whenever possible. Being close to a hotel doesn’t necessarily mean being close to anything useful.

Third, don’t assume that an Italian restaurant will provide a decent meal. Sometimes a $20 Lean Cuisine is exactly what you’re going to get, only with a longer walk and a much larger bill.

Fourth, Saturday night entertainment is not guaranteed. Sometimes you can search and search and still come up empty.

And finally, if you’re sitting in a hotel room watching the Sharter Show because you’ve run out of things to do, perhaps it’s time to reconsider your current location.

We never asked for a Wilkes-Barre vacation.

We didn’t book it, plan it, or choose it.

And after everything we experienced, I think we can safely say that it wasn’t exactly the destination we would have selected ourselves.

At least we got to see Arrested Development along the way.

The original plan was Rochester to Atlanta.

The actual adventure was a forced landing, a transportation nightmare, a disappointing Italian dinner, an entertainment drought, and an unexpected concert.

Not exactly what we had in mind.

But certainly a story worth telling.

And if anyone ever asks whether we would recommend spending a weekend in Wilkes-Barre, the answer might depend on how much they enjoy walking a mile for a $20 frozen dinner and watching the Sharter Show on Saturday night.

Personally, I’d rather take my chances with the FAA.
